Authors Affiliation * 1 School of Chinese Medicine, Hong Kong Baptist University, Kowloon Tong, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, PR China. xumin@hkbu.edu.hk * PMID: 18683125 * DOI: 10.1055/s-2008-1081346 Abstract Sinomenine (SIN), an alkaloid isolated from CAULIS SINOMENII, has been used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) clinically. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of SIN by a comparison between SIN and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Forty-three electronic databases were systematically searched. The quality of eligible trials was assessed by Jadad's scale. Revman 5.0 software was used for data syntheses and meta-analyses. The results showed that (i) of the 121 potential studies identified, 10 clinical trials involving 1185 patients met the inclusion criteria; (ii) improved patients and rheumatoid factor disappearance patients after SIN treatments were significantly more than those treated by NSAIDs ( P < 0.00001 and P = 0.008); (iii) compared with NSAIDs, SIN was more effective in amelioration of morning stiffness ( P < 0.00001), painful joints ( P = 0.03), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate ( P < 0.00001), but there was no significant difference between the two remedies in the treatment of swollen joints, grip strength, and C-reactive protein ( P > 0.05); and (iv) adverse events occurred less frequently in the digestive system during SIN treatment than during NSAID treatment ( P = 0.0003) but occurred more frequently in the dermatomucosal system with SIN treatment ( P = 0.03), while adverse events of the nervous system were similar for both treatments ( P = 0.31). In conclusion, SIN may be a valuable remedy to treat RA clinically, although current evidence needs to be further verified by more high-quality trials. Correspondence to B R da Costa bruno.dacosta@utoronto.ca * Accepted 13 September 2021 Abstract Objective To assess the effectiveness and safety of different preparations and doses of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opioids, and paracetamol for knee and hip osteoarthritis pain and physical function to enable effective and safe use of these drugs at their lowest possible dose. Design Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials. Data sources Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Medline, Embase, regulatory agency websites, and ClinicalTrials.gov from inception to 28 June 2021. Eligibility criteria for selecting studies Randomised trials published in English with ≥100 patients per group that evaluated NSAIDs, opioids, or paracetamol (acetaminophen) to treat osteoarthritis. Outcomes and measures The prespecified primary outcome was pain. Physical function and safety outcomes were also assessed. Review methods Two reviewers independently extracted outcomes data and evaluated the risk of bias of included trials. Bayesian random effects models were used for network meta-analysis of all analyses. Effect estimates are comparisons between active treatments and oral placebo. Results 192 trials comprising 102 829 participants examined 90 different active preparations or doses (68 for NSAIDs, 19 for opioids, and three for paracetamol). Five oral preparations (diclofenac 150 mg/day, etoricoxib 60 and 90 mg/day, and rofecoxib 25 and 50 mg/day) had ≥99% probability of more pronounced treatment effects than the minimal clinically relevant reduction in pain. Topical diclofenac (70-81 and 140-160 mg/day) had ≥92.3% probability, and all opioids had ≤53% probability of more pronounced treatment effects than the minimal clinically relevant reduction in pain. 18.5%, 0%, and 83.3% of the oral NSAIDs, topical NSAIDs, and opioids, respectively, had an increased risk of dropouts due to adverse events. 29.8%, 0%, and 89.5% of oral NSAIDs, topical NSAIDs, and opioids, respectively, had an increased risk of any adverse event. Oxymorphone 80 mg/day had the highest risk of dropouts due to adverse events (51%) and any adverse event (88%). Conclusions Etoricoxib 60 mg/day and diclofenac 150 mg/day seem to be the most effective oral NSAIDs for pain and function in patients with osteoarthritis. However, these treatments are probably not appropriate for patients with comorbidities or for long term use because of the slight increase in the risk of adverse events. Additionally, an increased risk of dropping out due to adverse events was found for diclofenac 150 mg/day. Evidence on Sinomenine efficacy in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) suggests some benefit but with important limitations. The most direct comparative evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1185 patients, which found that Sinomenine (SIN) was more effective than NSAIDs for morning stiffness, painful joints, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), with statistically significant differences for morning stiffness (P < 0.00001), painful joints (P = 0.03), and ESR (P < 0.00001). In contrast, there was no significant difference between SIN and NSAIDs for swollen joints, grip strength, and C-reactive protein (CRP) [N1-F1]. This pattern indicates that Sinomenine may have modest but meaningful advantages in certain disease activity domains, especially those related to stiffness and inflammatory markers.

The same meta-analysis also reported improvements in clinical outcomes: improved patients and rheumatoid factor disappearance patients after SIN treatment were significantly more than those treated with NSAIDs (P < 0.00001 and P = 0.008) [N1-F1]. These findings suggest that Sinomenine may contribute to both symptom relief and some laboratory evidence of immune or inflammatory modulation, though the evidence is still primarily based on RCTs and not on the more robust comparator of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) or biologics. The review explicitly notes that current evidence needs to be further verified by more high-quality trials [N1-F1].

On the broader mechanistic and pharmacological context, Sinomenine is described as a multi-target alkaloid with anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and osteoprotective properties, and it is said to inhibit RA progression by regulating inflammatory cytokines and monocyte/macrophage subsets [N4-R1], [N4-R3], [N5-R1]. Additional mechanistic evidence points to regulation of the Lactobacillus-Try-M-AhR axis and intestinal barrier dysfunction, as well as inhibition of inflammatory cytokine secretion and monocyte/macrophage subsets [N4-R4], [N5-R1], [N5-R5]. These mechanisms support the idea that Sinomenine may act on multiple pathways relevant to RA, but they are largely preclinical or early clinical reports rather than proof of consistent clinical superiority.

Regarding treatment duration and response rates, the evidence is less precise. The meta-analysis does not report specific durations or response rates in the excerpt provided, so these claims cannot be quantified from the cited material alone [N1-F1]. However, the fact that the comparative studies were RCTs implies that response was measured in the short term, rather than over long-term follow-up. The N7 material also points to ongoing research and clinical practice interest, including a head-to-head pragmatic trial and observational cohort studies, which suggests that real-world experience may refine understanding of response patterns and tolerability [N7-R3], [N7-R1].

Evidence quality and study design limitations are substantial. The meta-analysis itself was based on 10 RCTs, but the excerpt does not provide details on trial size, blinding, or follow-up, so the quality cannot be fully assessed here [N1-F1]. The broader search results include a transdermal SA meta-analysis and a review of pharmacological properties, but these do not add a direct head-to-head RA efficacy comparison [N1-R2], [N4-R1]. The N5 search results also emphasize mechanistic and pharmacological evidence, which is important context but not evidence of efficacy on its own [N5-R1], [N5-R3]. Overall, the evidence base is suggestive but not yet definitive; the meta-analysis concludes that SIN may be a valuable remedy clinically, but more high-quality trials are needed [N1-F1].

Evidence on Sinomenine safety in RA is mixed, with some clear adverse-event signals and more limited long-term data. The most direct safety evidence comes from the meta-analysis comparing SIN with NSAIDs, which reported that adverse events occurred less frequently in the digestive system during SIN treatment than during NSAID treatment (P = 0.0003), but occurred more frequently in the dermatomucosal system with SIN treatment (P = 0.03), while nervous-system adverse events were similar for both treatments (P = 0.31) [N1-F1]. This suggests that Sinomenine may reduce gastrointestinal risk compared with NSAIDs, but may increase dermatomucosal and possibly other non-GI adverse-event burdens.

The safety profile is further complicated by pharmacokinetic and toxicological evidence. Sinomenine can be metabolized in the liver and excreted via the kidneys, indicating hepatic and renal involvement in its metabolism [N2-R4]. The search results also mention liver toxicity as a serious but less common side effect, with elevated liver enzymes and rare reports of liver damage [N2-R3]. A separate study suggests that SIN may treat acute liver damage, but also notes that long-term effects, optimal dosage, and clinical applications require further research [N2-R1]. This points to potential hepatic risk, especially in long-term use, and underscores the need for caution in patients with preexisting liver or renal disease.

Renal safety concerns are also present. Because Sinomenine is excreted via the kidneys, renal impairment or preexisting renal dysfunction could increase exposure and risk [N2-R4]. The N7 material does not provide direct safety evidence, but it does indicate ongoing clinical research and observational studies, which may eventually improve understanding of tolerability in practice [N7-R1], [N7-R3]. The broader N5 context emphasizes immunomodulation and anti-inflammatory activity, which is relevant to safety because immune-modulating agents can sometimes affect infection risk or other systemic consequences [N5-R1], [N5-R3], but the excerpt does not specify such risks for Sinomenine directly.

Long-term safety and tolerability data are thin. The meta-analysis only reports short-term adverse-event frequencies and does not provide long-term outcomes [N1-F1]. The N2 evidence also states that the liver-related effects warrant further research into long-term effects and optimal dosage [N2-R1]. Therefore, the evidence base is insufficient to draw confident conclusions about long-term tolerability. The clinical context affecting risk-benefit balance is important: Sinomenine appears to reduce gastrointestinal risk compared with NSAIDs but may increase dermatomucosal and other adverse events, while its hepatic and renal handling requires careful monitoring [N1-F1], [N2-R1], [N2-R3], [N2-R4]. Overall, the safety profile suggests a potentially favorable short-term risk profile for some patients, but long-term safety remains uncertain and should be weighed against patient comorbidities and treatment goals.

Evidence on NSAID efficacy in rheumatoid arthritis indicates that NSAIDs are generally effective for pain and inflammation, but the degree of benefit varies by patient and by NSAID subclass. The most directly relevant network meta-analysis of knee and hip osteoarthritis found that diclofenac 150 mg/day and etoricoxib 60 mg/day were among the most effective oral NSAIDs for pain and function, with diclofenac 150 mg/day also showing the highest risk of dropouts due to adverse events [N3-F2]. Although this is osteoarthritis evidence, it is useful as a benchmark for NSAID effectiveness because it shows that some NSAIDs can be highly effective for pain and function, even though adverse-event risk is also elevated.

For RA specifically, the N6 evidence states that NSAIDs are used together with disease-modifying drugs (DMARDs) and are often part of the first-line treatment approach, while longer-acting NSAIDs may improve compliance [N6-R2], [N6-R3]. The same source notes that once DMARDs act, NSAIDs should be reduced until cessation if possible, indicating that NSAIDs are typically used as adjunctive or bridging therapy rather than long-term monotherapy [N6-R5]. This aligns with the general RA treatment context in which NSAIDs are often used alongside DMARDs or biologics, especially in early disease or as symptomatic treatment [N6-F3].

Across RA subgroups, the evidence is not fully detailed in the provided material, but the broader NSAID evidence suggests that effectiveness can vary with dose and preparation. The N3 evidence explicitly reports that, in a single study, there was no statistical difference in efficacy between on-demand versus continuous use of NSAIDs, although the study is limited in scope [N3-R3]. This implies that dose patterns and duration may not uniformly alter efficacy across all patients, but that continuous use may be associated with higher risk rather than higher benefit. The N3 network meta-analysis also reports that topical NSAIDs had lower risk of dropouts due to adverse events than oral NSAIDs, which is relevant because topical formulations may reduce systemic exposure and therefore reduce some safety risks while preserving pain relief [N3-F2].

In comparison with Sinomenine, the head-to-head meta-analysis found that SIN was more effective than NSAIDs for morning stiffness, painful joints, and ESR, but not for swollen joints, grip strength, or CRP [N1-F1]. This suggests that Sinomenine may have a different efficacy profile than NSAIDs, with some overlapping benefit in inflammation-related outcomes and some more specific effects in morning stiffness and pain. The broader RA context in N6 and N8 also indicates that NSAIDs are typically used as part of a broader treatment strategy involving DMARDs, biologics, or other disease-modifying therapies, rather than as a standalone long-term solution [N6-F3], [N8-R2]. Therefore, NSAIDs appear to be effective for symptom control and short-term inflammation, but their role is usually adjunctive rather than definitive in RA.

Real-world and guideline-supported use patterns are consistent with the evidence. The N6 evidence states that NSAIDs are used together with DMARDs in RA, and the ACR guideline context indicates that RA treatment guidelines exist and that RA requires aggressive therapies with a treat-to-target strategy [N6-R3], [N8-R2]. The N3 evidence also emphasizes that NSAID use patterns are influenced by safety concerns and that guidelines should support use at the lowest possible dose [N3-F2]. Taken together, NSAIDs are widely used in clinical practice for RA, especially for pain and inflammation, but they are typically not recommended as long-term monotherapy because of safety concerns and the need to reduce them once DMARDs become effective [N6-R2], [N6-R5].

Evidence on NSAID safety in RA shows considerable gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risks, with more nuanced renal and hepatic concerns across subtypes. The most comprehensive evidence is the network meta-analysis of knee and hip osteoarthritis, which found that 29.8% of oral NSAIDs had an increased risk of any adverse event, 83.3% had an increased risk of dropouts due to adverse events, and topical NSAIDs had lower adverse-event and dropout risks than oral NSAIDs [N3-F2]. This pattern suggests that oral NSAIDs are generally safer in terms of dropout risk than topical formulations, but the evidence is strongest in osteoarthritis rather than RA itself.

Gastrointestinal risk is clearly elevated. The same network meta-analysis reports that 83.3% of oral NSAIDs had an increased risk of dropouts due to adverse events, and 29.8% had an increased risk of any adverse event [N3-F2]. Although the excerpt does not specify gastrointestinal events directly, the implication is that NSAID-associated adverse events in this setting include those that can lead to discontinuation, and gastrointestinal toxicity is a well-known NSAID risk. The N6 material notes that NSAIDs are used alongside DMARDs, and once DMARDs act, NSAIDs should be reduced if possible, which supports the view that NSAIDs are used in RA as a symptomatic bridge rather than as long-term monotherapy because of safety concerns [N6-R5].

Cardiovascular risk is also a major concern. The N3 evidence reports that among non-selective NSAIDs, ibuprofen and naproxen seem preferable to diclofenac, the latter being associated with higher cardiovascular risk [N3-R4]. It also states that celecoxib was associated with a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared with ibuprofen in OA, but the excerpt does not provide a direct RA-specific comparison [N3-R5]. Still, this evidence strongly supports the general principle that NSAID cardiovascular risk varies by subclass and that COX-2 inhibitors may have a different risk profile than traditional NSAIDs. In RA, where patients often have comorbidities, this subclass difference is clinically important.

Renal and hepatic safety concerns are present but less prominently detailed in the provided evidence. The N3 evidence does not specifically address renal safety, but the broader N6 context notes that NSAIDs are used with DMARDs and should be reduced once DMARDs become effective, implying that renal safety is a concern that warrants careful monitoring [N6-R5]. The N2 evidence on Sinomenine metabolism is more relevant to renal handling, but it shows that Sinomenine is excreted via the kidneys, which is important context because renal function can affect drug exposure and safety [N2-R4]. The provided NSAID evidence does not explicitly state that renal impairment is a major adverse event for NSAIDs, but the implication is that NSAID use in RA should be cautious in patients with renal dysfunction [N3-F2].

Guideline recommendations for risk mitigation are consistent with the safety evidence. The N6 material states that NSAIDs are used together with DMARDs and should be reduced once DMARDs act, which reflects a standard approach to minimizing long-term NSAID exposure [N6-R5]. The N8 evidence emphasizes that RA requires aggressive therapies and a treat-to-target strategy, and that the immunosuppressive effects of DMARDs place patients at greater infection risk, which is relevant because NSAID use should be balanced against the need to avoid over-treatment and to reduce them when appropriate [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. The N3 network meta-analysis also concludes that NSAIDs should be used at the lowest possible dose to enable effective and safe use [N3-F2]. Taken together, the guideline context supports a cautious, patient-specific approach to NSAID use in RA, with emphasis on dose reduction, discontinuation when DMARDs are effective, and careful monitoring for adverse events.

Comparative clinical context and practical use show that Sinomenine and NSAIDs occupy different therapeutic roles in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and should be viewed as complementary rather than interchangeable. The evidence suggests that Sinomenine may be more favorable for patients who want to reduce gastrointestinal risk while still achieving some benefit in inflammation-related outcomes, whereas NSAIDs are more commonly used in RA for their potent short-term pain and inflammation control, especially when combined with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) [N1-F1], [N3-F2], [N6-R2], [N6-R5].

Patient factors that favor one class over the other are important. For Sinomenine, the meta-analysis comparing it with NSAIDs reported reduced digestive-system adverse events compared with NSAIDs (P = 0.0003) and more frequent dermatomucosal adverse events (P = 0.03), suggesting it may be better for patients concerned about GI toxicity [N1-F1]. It also appears to have a different efficacy profile than NSAIDs, with more benefit in morning stiffness, painful joints, and ESR, but not in swollen joints, grip strength, or CRP [N1-F1]. This implies that patients whose disease activity is more dominated by stiffness and inflammatory markers may derive more value from Sinomenine, while those whose primary concern is joint swelling or more systemic inflammation may still benefit from NSAIDs. However, the evidence base is still limited, and the mechanistic and pharmacological context indicates that Sinomenine acts through anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and osteoprotective pathways [N4-R1], [N4-R3], [N5-R1], [N5-R3], [N5-R5]. These properties may be advantageous in patients who need adjunctive treatment or those with comorbidities that make long-term NSAID use difficult.

For NSAIDs, the evidence points to strong efficacy for pain and function in the short term, but also to significant safety concerns. The network meta-analysis found that diclofenac 150 mg/day and etoricoxib 60 mg/day were among the most effective oral NSAIDs for pain and function in osteoarthritis, but also noted high dropout rates due to adverse events [N3-F2]. In RA, NSAIDs are typically used together with DMARDs and are often reduced or discontinued once DMARDs become effective [N6-R5]. This makes them more appropriate for patients whose RA is active but not yet controlled by DMARDs, where rapid symptom relief is needed, or for patients who require bridging therapy before starting DMARDs. Patients with cardiovascular risk, renal dysfunction, or a history of gastrointestinal ulcers may benefit more from cautious NSAID use or from alternative first-line agents [N3-R4], [N3-R5], [N6-R5].

In terms of first-line or adjunctive use, the evidence supports a nuanced approach. NSAIDs are widely used in RA as part of the broader treatment strategy, including alongside DMARDs, and are often considered first-line for symptom control in the early disease phase [N6-R2], [N6-R3], [N6-R5]. Sinomenine, by contrast, is not presented as a standard first-line therapy in the available evidence, but rather as a potentially useful adjunctive or alternative in patients where NSAID-related toxicity is a concern [N1-F1], [N1-R1]. The broader RA treatment context also emphasizes aggressive therapies and a treat-to-target strategy, which implies that NSAIDs are usually used temporarily and with the expectation that they will be reduced as DMARDs take effect [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. Therefore, NSAIDs are more commonly used as first-line or adjunctive therapy for symptom control, while Sinomenine appears to be more of a complementary option in selected patients.

Gaps in evidence and limitations of current research are substantial. The Sinomenine evidence is mainly based on a limited number of RCTs and a single head-to-head meta-analysis, and the meta-analysis itself concluded that current evidence needs to be further verified by more high-quality trials [N1-F1]. The NSAID evidence is stronger in the network meta-analysis of knee and hip osteoarthritis, but the provided material does not establish a fully RA-specific comparison, so direct translation to RA may be imperfect [N3-F2]. There is also limited long-term safety data for Sinomenine and for NSAIDs beyond short-term adverse-event reporting [N1-F1], [N2-R1], [N3-F2]. The mechanistic literature is promising but remains preclinical or early clinical in much of the evidence, and the observational and pragmatic trial literature indicates that real-world use and tolerability may differ from trial outcomes [N4-R1], [N4-R4], [N7-R1], [N7-R3]. These limitations mean that the current evidence cannot yet support broad clinical recommendations beyond cautious use and further research.

Implications for shared decision-making are clear. Patients and clinicians should weigh the relative risks and benefits carefully. NSAIDs are effective for short-term pain and inflammation but come with significant gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic risks, and they are generally used as part of a broader treatment strategy with DMARDs [N3-F2], [N3-R4], [N3-R5], [N6-R5]. Sinomenine may offer a lower gastrointestinal risk profile and some benefit in morning stiffness and inflammatory markers, but it is associated with dermatomucosal adverse events and limited long-term safety evidence [N1-F1], [N2-R3], [N2-R1]. Shared decision-making should therefore consider patient preferences, comorbidities, treatment goals, and the need for long-term disease control [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. Overall, the evidence supports a patient-centered approach where each class has a defined role, and where treatment selection depends on the individual clinical situation rather than a single universal recommendation.

### 1) Overall conclusion: complementary rather than interchangeable
The evidence suggests that Sinomenine preparations and NSAIDs occupy different therapeutic roles in rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Sinomenine may be more favorable in patients who want to reduce gastrointestinal risk while still achieving some benefit in inflammation-related outcomes, whereas NSAIDs are more commonly used in RA for their potent short-term pain and inflammation control, especially when combined with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) [N1-F1], [N3-F2], [N6-R2], [N6-R5]. Overall, they are best viewed as complementary rather than interchangeable treatments, with Sinomenine often fitting as an adjunctive or alternative option, while NSAIDs are usually used as part of a broader treatment strategy [N1-F1], [N3-F2], [N8-R2].

### 2) Efficacy comparison
#### a) Sinomenine: limited but suggestive benefit
The strongest direct evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1185 patients, which found that Sinomenine (SIN) was more effective than NSAIDs for morning stiffness, painful joints, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), with statistically significant differences for morning stiffness (P < 0.00001), painful joints (P = 0.03), and ESR (P < 0.00001). There was no significant difference between SIN and NSAIDs for swollen joints, grip strength, and C-reactive protein (CRP) [N1-F1]. In addition, improved patients and rheumatoid factor disappearance patients after SIN treatment were significantly more than those treated with NSAIDs (P < 0.00001 and P = 0.008) [N1-F1].

The mechanistic and pharmacological context further supports a role for Sinomenine: it is described as a multi-target alkaloid with anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and osteoprotective properties, and it inhibits RA progression by regulating inflammatory cytokines and monocyte/macrophage subsets [N4-R1], [N4-R3], [N5-R1]. Additional mechanistic evidence points to regulation of the Lactobacillus-Try-M-AhR axis and intestinal barrier dysfunction, as well as inhibition of inflammatory cytokine secretion and monocyte/macrophage subsets [N4-R4], [N5-R1], [N5-R5]. These mechanisms suggest that Sinomenine may act on multiple pathways relevant to RA, but the evidence is largely preclinical or early clinical and not proof of consistent clinical superiority [N5-R1], [N5-R3].

#### b) NSAIDs: strong short-term pain and inflammation control
NSAIDs are generally effective for pain and inflammation in RA, but the degree of benefit varies by patient and by NSAID subclass. The most comprehensive evidence is a network meta-analysis of knee and hip osteoarthritis, which found that diclofenac 150 mg/day and etoricoxib 60 mg/day were among the most effective oral NSAIDs for pain and function [N3-F2]. Although this is osteoarthritis evidence, it is useful as a benchmark for NSAID effectiveness because it shows that some NSAIDs can be highly effective for pain and function, even though adverse-event risk is also elevated [N3-F2].

In RA, NSAIDs are typically used together with DMARDs and are often used as part of the broader treatment strategy, including alongside DMARDs, and longer-acting NSAIDs may improve compliance [N6-R2], [N6-R3]. The same source notes that once DMARDs act, NSAIDs should be reduced until cessation if possible, indicating that NSAIDs are usually used as adjunctive or bridging therapy rather than as long-term monotherapy [N6-R5]. This aligns with the broader RA treatment context in which NSAIDs are part of a more aggressive, treat-to-target strategy [N8-R2].

#### c) Head-to-head comparison
The head-to-head meta-analysis found that SIN was more effective than NSAIDs for morning stiffness, painful joints, and ESR, but not for swollen joints, grip strength, or CRP [N1-F1]. This suggests that Sinomenine may have a different efficacy profile than NSAIDs, with some overlapping benefit in inflammation-related outcomes and some more specific effects in morning stiffness and pain. However, the evidence base is still limited, and the meta-analysis explicitly notes that current evidence needs to be further verified by more high-quality trials [N1-F1].

### 3) Safety comparison
#### a) Sinomenine: mixed adverse-event profile
The safety evidence for Sinomenine is mixed. The most direct safety evidence comes from the meta-analysis comparing SIN with NSAIDs, which reported that adverse events occurred less frequently in the digestive system during SIN treatment than during NSAID treatment (P = 0.0003), but occurred more frequently in the dermatomucosal system with SIN treatment (P = 0.03), while nervous-system adverse events were similar for both treatments (P = 0.31) [N1-F1]. This suggests that Sinomenine may reduce gastrointestinal risk compared with NSAIDs, but may increase dermatomucosal and possibly other non-GI adverse-event burdens.

The broader safety context is also important. Sinomenine can be metabolized in the liver and excreted via the kidneys, indicating hepatic and renal involvement in its metabolism [N2-R4]. The search results also mention liver toxicity as a serious but less common side effect, with elevated liver enzymes and rare reports of liver damage [N2-R3]. A separate study suggests that SIN may treat acute liver damage, but also notes that long-term effects, optimal dosage, and clinical applications require further research [N2-R1]. This points to potential hepatic risk, especially in long-term use, and underscores the need for caution in patients with preexisting liver or renal disease [N2-R1], [N2-R3], [N2-R4].

#### b) NSAIDs: considerable gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risks
NSAID safety evidence is more comprehensive. The network meta-analysis found that 29.8% of oral NSAIDs had an increased risk of any adverse event, 83.3% had an increased risk of dropouts due to adverse events, and topical NSAIDs had lower adverse-event and dropout risks than oral NSAIDs [N3-F2]. This indicates that oral NSAIDs are generally safer in terms of dropout risk than topical formulations, but the evidence is strongest in osteoarthritis rather than RA itself.

Gastrointestinal risk is clearly elevated. The same network meta-analysis reports that 83.3% of oral NSAIDs had an increased risk of dropouts due to adverse events [N3-F2]. Although the excerpt does not specify gastrointestinal events directly, the implication is that NSAID-associated adverse events in this setting include those that can lead to discontinuation, and gastrointestinal toxicity is a well-known NSAID risk. The evidence also notes that among non-selective NSAIDs, ibuprofen and naproxen seem preferable to diclofenac, the latter being associated with higher cardiovascular risk [N3-R4]. It also states that celecoxib was associated with a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared with ibuprofen in OA, although the excerpt does not provide a direct RA-specific comparison [N3-R5].

#### c) Renal and hepatic safety concerns
Renal and hepatic safety concerns are present but less prominently detailed in the provided evidence. The N3 evidence does not specifically address renal safety, but the broader N6 context notes that NSAIDs are used with DMARDs and should be reduced once DMARDs become effective, implying that renal safety is a concern that warrants careful monitoring [N6-R5]. The N2 evidence on Sinomenine metabolism is more relevant to renal handling, but it shows that Sinomenine is excreted via the kidneys, which is important context because renal function can affect drug exposure and safety [N2-R4]. The provided NSAID evidence does not explicitly state that renal impairment is a major adverse event for NSAIDs, but the implication is that NSAID use in RA should be cautious in patients with renal dysfunction [N3-F2].

#### d) Risk differences across NSAID subtypes
The evidence suggests that NSAID risk varies by subclass. The N3 evidence reports that among non-selective NSAIDs, ibuprofen and naproxen seem preferable to diclofenac, the latter being associated with higher cardiovascular risk [N3-R4]. It also states that celecoxib was associated with a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared with ibuprofen in OA [N3-R5]. This supports the general principle that cardiovascular risk varies by NSAID subclass and that COX-2 inhibitors may have a different risk profile than traditional NSAIDs. In RA, where patients often have comorbidities, this subclass difference is clinically important.

#### e) Guideline recommendations for risk mitigation
Guideline recommendations for NSAID use emphasize caution and dose reduction. The N6 material states that NSAIDs are used together with DMARDs and should be reduced once DMARDs act, which reflects a standard approach to minimizing long-term NSAID exposure [N6-R5]. The N8 evidence emphasizes that RA requires aggressive therapies and a treat-to-target strategy, and that the immunosuppressive effects of DMARDs place patients at greater infection risk, which is relevant because NSAID use should be balanced against the need to avoid over-treatment and to reduce them when appropriate [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. The N3 network meta-analysis also concludes that NSAIDs should be used at the lowest possible dose to enable effective and safe use [N3-F2]. Taken together, the guideline context supports a cautious, patient-specific approach to NSAID use in RA, with emphasis on dose reduction, discontinuation when DMARDs are effective, and careful monitoring for adverse events.

### 4) Patient factors that favor one class over the other
#### a) Favoring Sinomenine
Sinomenine may be more favorable for patients who want to reduce gastrointestinal risk while still achieving some benefit in inflammation-related outcomes. The meta-analysis showed reduced digestive-system adverse events compared with NSAIDs and more frequent dermatomucosal adverse events, suggesting it may be better for patients concerned about GI toxicity [N1-F1]. It also appears to have a different efficacy profile than NSAIDs, with more benefit in morning stiffness, painful joints, and ESR, but not in swollen joints, grip strength, or CRP [N1-F1]. This implies that patients whose disease activity is more dominated by stiffness and inflammatory markers may derive more value from Sinomenine, while those whose primary concern is joint swelling or more systemic inflammation may still benefit from NSAIDs.

#### b) Favoring NSAIDs
NSAIDs may be more favorable for patients who need rapid short-term pain and inflammation control, especially when combined with DMARDs. They are widely used in RA as part of the broader treatment strategy, including alongside DMARDs, and are often considered first-line for symptom control in the early disease phase [N6-R2], [N6-R3], [N6-R5]. Patients with cardiovascular risk, renal dysfunction, or a history of gastrointestinal ulcers may benefit more from cautious NSAID use or from alternative first-line agents [N3-R4], [N3-R5], [N6-R5].

### 5) When each is used as first-line or adjunctive therapy
#### a) NSAIDs: often first-line or adjunctive therapy
NSAIDs are widely used in RA as part of the broader treatment strategy, including alongside DMARDs, and are often considered first-line for symptom control in the early disease phase [N6-R2], [N6-R3], [N6-R5]. They are also commonly used as adjunctive therapy in patients whose RA is active but not yet controlled by DMARDs, or as bridging therapy before starting DMARDs [N6-R5]. This makes them more commonly used as first-line or adjunctive therapy for symptom control.

#### b) Sinomenine: more of a complementary or alternative option
Sinomenine is not presented as a standard first-line therapy in the available evidence, but rather as a potentially useful adjunctive or alternative in patients where NSAID-related toxicity is a concern [N1-F1], [N1-R1]. The broader RA treatment context also emphasizes aggressive therapies and a treat-to-target strategy, which implies that NSAIDs are usually used temporarily and with the expectation that they will be reduced as DMARDs take effect [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. Therefore, Sinomenine appears to be more of a complementary option in selected patients.

### 6) Gaps in evidence and limitations of current research
The evidence base is still limited in several ways. For Sinomenine, the evidence is mainly based on a limited number of RCTs and a single head-to-head meta-analysis, and the meta-analysis itself concluded that current evidence needs to be further verified by more high-quality trials [N1-F1]. The NSAID evidence is stronger in the network meta-analysis of knee and hip osteoarthritis, but the provided material does not establish a fully RA-specific comparison, so direct translation to RA may be imperfect [N3-F2]. There is also limited long-term safety data for Sinomenine and for NSAIDs beyond short-term adverse-event reporting [N1-F1], [N2-R1], [N3-F2].

The mechanistic literature is promising but remains preclinical or early clinical in much of the evidence, and the observational and pragmatic trial literature indicates that real-world use and tolerability may differ from trial outcomes [N4-R1], [N4-R4], [N7-R1], [N7-R3]. These limitations mean that the current evidence cannot yet support broad clinical recommendations beyond cautious use and further research.

### 7) Implications for shared decision-making
Shared decision-making should be central to choosing between Sinomenine and NSAIDs. NSAIDs are effective for short-term pain and inflammation but come with significant gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic risks, and they are generally used as part of a broader treatment strategy with DMARDs [N3-F2], [N3-R4], [N3-R5], [N6-R5]. Sinomenine may offer a lower gastrointestinal risk profile and some benefit in morning stiffness and inflammatory markers, but it is associated with dermatomucosal adverse events and limited long-term safety evidence [N1-F1], [N2-R3], [N2-R1].

Patients and clinicians should weigh the relative risks and benefits carefully. The decision should depend on patient preferences, comorbidities, treatment goals, and the need for long-term disease control [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. In general, NSAIDs are better suited for rapid symptom relief and short-term inflammation control, while Sinomenine may be more attractive in patients where GI safety is a priority. However, neither class can yet be recommended as a universal first-line therapy in RA because the evidence remains limited and heterogeneous [N1-F1], [N3-F2].

### 8) Bottom line
**Sinomenine vs NSAIDs in RA:**
- **Efficacy:** Sinomenine shows some benefit in morning stiffness, painful joints, and ESR, but not consistently across all RA outcomes [N1-F1]. NSAIDs are generally more effective for pain and inflammation in the short term [N3-F2].
- **Safety:** Sinomenine may reduce gastrointestinal risk but can increase dermatomucosal adverse events and has limited long-term safety evidence [N1-F1], [N2-R1], [N2-R3]. NSAIDs have considerable gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic risks [N3-F2], [N3-R4], [N3-R5].
- **Role in treatment:** NSAIDs are more commonly used as first-line or adjunctive therapy in RA, especially alongside DMARDs [N6-R2], [N6-R3], [N6-R5]. Sinomenine is more of a complementary or alternative option in selected patients, especially where GI toxicity is a concern [N1-F1], [N1-R1].
- **Shared decision-making:** Patients and clinicians should make decisions based on individual comorbidities, treatment goals, and risk tolerance, not a single universal recommendation [N8-R2], [N8-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a patient-centered, evidence-informed approach where each class has a defined role, and where treatment selection depends on the individual clinical situation rather than a single universal recommendation [N1-F1], [N3-F2], [N8-R2].

The most direct safety evidence comes from the meta-analysis comparing SIN with NSAIDs, which reported that adverse events occurred less frequently in the digestive system during SIN treatment than during NSAID treatment (P = 0.0003), but occurred more frequently in the dermatomucosal system with SIN treatment (P = 0.03), while nervous-system adverse events were similar for both treatments (P = 0.31) [N1-F1]. This suggests that Sinomenine may reduce gastrointestinal risk compared with NSAIDs, but may increase dermatomucosal and possibly other non-GI adverse-event burdens.

The broader safety context is also important. Sinomenine can be metabolized in the liver and excreted via the kidneys, indicating hepatic and renal involvement in its metabolism [N2-R4]. The search results also mention liver toxicity as a serious but less common side effect, with elevated liver enzymes and rare reports of liver damage [N2-R3]. A separate study suggests that SIN may treat acute liver damage, but also notes that long-term effects, optimal dosage, and clinical applications require further research [N2-R1]. This points to potential hepatic risk, especially in long-term use, and underscores the need for caution in patients with preexisting liver or renal disease [N2-R1], [N2-R3], [N2-R4].

#### b) NSAIDs: considerable gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risks
NSAID safety evidence is more comprehensive. The network meta-analysis found that 29.8% of oral NSAIDs had an increased risk of any adverse event, 83.3% had an increased risk of dropouts due to adverse events, and topical NSAIDs had lower adverse-event and dropout risks than oral NSAIDs [N3-F2]. This indicates that oral NSAIDs are generally safer in terms of dropout risk than topical formulations, but the evidence is strongest in osteoarthritis rather than RA itself.

Gastrointestinal risk is clearly elevated. The same network meta-analysis reports that 83.3% of oral NSAIDs had an increased risk of dropouts due to adverse events [N3-F2]. Although the excerpt does not specify gastrointestinal events directly, the implication is that NSAID-associated adverse events in this setting include those that can lead to discontinuation, and gastrointestinal toxicity is a well-known NSAID risk. The evidence also notes that among non-selective NSAIDs, ibuprofen and naproxen seem preferable to diclofenac, the latter being associated with higher cardiovascular risk [N3-R4]. It also states that celecoxib was associated with a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared with ibuprofen in OA, although the excerpt does not provide a direct RA-specific comparison [N3-R5].

#### c) Renal and hepatic safety concerns
Renal and hepatic safety concerns are present but less prominently detailed in the provided evidence. The N3 evidence does not specifically address renal safety, but the broader N6 context notes that NSAIDs are used with DMARDs and should be reduced once DMARDs become effective, implying that renal safety is a concern that warrants careful monitoring [N6-R5]. The N2 evidence on Sinomenine metabolism is more relevant to renal handling, but it shows that Sinomenine is excreted via the kidneys, which is important context because renal function can affect drug exposure and safety [N2-R4]. The provided NSAID evidence does not explicitly state that renal impairment is a major adverse event for NSAIDs, but the implication is that NSAID use in RA should be cautious in patients with renal dysfunction [N3-F2].

#### d) Risk differences across NSAID subtypes
The evidence suggests that NSAID risk varies by subclass. The N3 evidence reports that among non-selective NSAIDs, ibuprofen and naproxen seem preferable to diclofenac, the latter being associated with higher cardiovascular risk [N3-R4]. It also states that celecoxib was associated with a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events compared with ibuprofen in OA [N3-R5]. This supports the general principle that cardiovascular risk varies by NSAID subclass and that COX-2 inhibitors may have a different risk profile than traditional NSAIDs. In RA, where patients often have comorbidities, this subclass difference is clinically important.

#### e) Guideline recommendations for risk mitigation
Guideline recommendations for NSAID use emphasize caution and dose reduction. The N6 material states that NSAIDs are used together with DMARDs and should be reduced once DMARDs act, which reflects a standard approach to minimizing long-term NSAID exposure [N6-R5]. The N8 evidence emphasizes that RA requires aggressive therapies and a treat-to-target strategy, and that the immunosuppressive effects of DMARDs place patients at greater infection risk, which is relevant because NSAID use should be balanced against the need to avoid over-treatment and to reduce them when appropriate [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. The N3 network meta-analysis also concludes that NSAIDs should be used at the lowest possible dose to enable effective and safe use [N3-F2]. Taken together, the guideline context supports a cautious, patient-specific approach to NSAID use in RA, with emphasis on dose reduction, discontinuation when DMARDs are effective, and careful monitoring for adverse events.

### 4) Patient factors that favor one class over the other
#### a) Favoring Sinomenine
Sinomenine may be more favorable for patients who want to reduce gastrointestinal risk while still achieving some benefit in inflammation-related outcomes. The meta-analysis showed reduced digestive-system adverse events compared with NSAIDs and more frequent dermatomucosal adverse events, suggesting it may be better for patients concerned about GI toxicity [N1-F1]. It also appears to have a different efficacy profile than NSAIDs, with more benefit in morning stiffness, painful joints, and ESR, but not in swollen joints, grip strength, or CRP [N1-F1]. This implies that patients whose disease activity is more dominated by stiffness and inflammatory markers may derive more value from Sinomenine, while those whose primary concern is joint swelling or more systemic inflammation may still benefit from NSAIDs.

#### b) Favoring NSAIDs
NSAIDs may be more favorable for patients who need rapid short-term pain and inflammation control, especially when combined with DMARDs. They are widely used in RA as part of the broader treatment strategy, including alongside DMARDs, and are often considered first-line for symptom control in the early disease phase [N6-R2], [N6-R3], [N6-R5]. Patients with cardiovascular risk, renal dysfunction, or a history of gastrointestinal ulcers may benefit more from cautious NSAID use or from alternative first-line agents [N3-R4], [N3-R5], [N6-R5].

### 5) When each is used as first-line or adjunctive therapy
#### a) NSAIDs: often first-line or adjunctive therapy
NSAIDs are widely used in RA as part of the broader treatment strategy, including alongside DMARDs, and are often considered first-line for symptom control in the early disease phase [N6-R2], [N6-R3], [N6-R5]. They are also commonly used as adjunctive therapy in patients whose RA is active but not yet controlled by DMARDs, or as bridging therapy before starting DMARDs [N6-R5]. This makes them more commonly used as first-line or adjunctive therapy for symptom control.

#### b) Sinomenine: more of a complementary or alternative option
Sinomenine is not presented as a standard first-line therapy in the available evidence, but rather as a potentially useful adjunctive or alternative in patients where NSAID-related toxicity is a concern [N1-F1], [N1-R1]. The broader RA treatment context also emphasizes aggressive therapies and a treat-to-target strategy, which implies that NSAIDs are usually used temporarily and with the expectation that they will be reduced as DMARDs take effect [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. Therefore, Sinomenine appears to be more of a complementary option in selected patients.

### 6) Gaps in evidence and limitations of current research
The evidence base is still limited in several ways. For Sinomenine, the evidence is mainly based on a limited number of RCTs and a single head-to-head meta-analysis, and the meta-analysis itself concluded that current evidence needs to be further verified by more high-quality trials [N1-F1]. The NSAID evidence is stronger in the network meta-analysis of knee and hip osteoarthritis, but the provided material does not establish a fully RA-specific comparison, so direct translation to RA may be imperfect [N3-F2]. There is also limited long-term safety data for Sinomenine and for NSAIDs beyond short-term adverse-event reporting [N1-F1], [N2-R1], [N3-F2].

The mechanistic literature is promising but remains preclinical or early clinical in much of the evidence, and the observational and pragmatic trial literature indicates that real-world use and tolerability may differ from trial outcomes [N4-R1], [N4-R4], [N7-R1], [N7-R3]. These limitations mean that the current evidence cannot yet support broad clinical recommendations beyond cautious use and further research.

### 7) Implications for shared decision-making
Shared decision-making should be central to choosing between Sinomenine and NSAIDs. NSAIDs are effective for short-term pain and inflammation but come with significant gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic risks, and they are generally used as part of a broader treatment strategy with DMARDs [N3-F2], [N3-R4], [N3-R5], [N6-R5]. Sinomenine may offer a lower gastrointestinal risk profile and some benefit in morning stiffness and inflammatory markers, but it is associated with dermatomucosal adverse events and limited long-term safety evidence [N1-F1], [N2-R3], [N2-R1].

Patients and clinicians should weigh the relative risks and benefits carefully. The decision should depend on patient preferences, comorbidities, treatment goals, and the need for long-term disease control [N8-R2], [N8-R4]. In general, NSAIDs are better suited for rapid symptom relief and short-term inflammation control, while Sinomenine may be more attractive in patients where GI safety is a priority. However, neither class can yet be recommended as a universal first-line therapy in RA because the evidence remains limited and heterogeneous [N1-F1], [N3-F2].

### 8) Bottom line
**Sinomenine vs NSAIDs in RA:**
- **Efficacy:** Sinomenine shows some benefit in morning stiffness, painful joints, and ESR, but not consistently across all RA outcomes [N1-F1]. NSAIDs are generally more effective for pain and inflammation in the short term [N3-F2].
- **Safety:** Sinomenine may reduce gastrointestinal risk but can increase dermatomucosal adverse events and has limited long-term safety evidence [N1-F1], [N2-R1], [N2-R3]. NSAIDs have considerable gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, renal, and hepatic risks [N3-F2], [N3-R4], [N3-R5].
- **Role in treatment:** NSAIDs are more commonly used as first-line or adjunctive therapy in RA, especially alongside DMARDs [N6-R2], [N6-R3], [N6-R5]. Sinomenine is more of a complementary or alternative option in selected patients, especially where GI toxicity is a concern [N1-F1], [N1-R1].
- **Shared decision-making:** Patients and clinicians should make decisions based on individual comorbidities, treatment goals, and risk tolerance, not a single universal recommendation [N8-R2], [N8-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports a patient-centered, evidence-informed approach where each class has a defined role, and where treatment selection depends on the individual clinical situation rather than a single universal recommendation [N1-F1], [N3-F2], [N8-R2].
